q: Which statement below is NOT correct?
options: Sensitive personal data includes political opinions and sexual preferences.
Sensitive personal data includes racial or ethnical origins and religious believes.
Sensitive personal data means any raw facts gathered about someone or something.
Sensitive personal data includes physical or mental health and criminal records.
explain: Raw facts gathered about someone or something is the definition of data. Sensitive personal data is personal data related to racial or ethnical origins, religious believes, political opinions, physical/mental health, sexual preferences, criminal records.

q: Which statement below is NOT correct?
options: Personal data is data about a living person who can be identified from the data.
Personal data is data about human beings.
Processing is anything you do with personal data, such as hold, store, gather, delete or modify.
Personal data is data about a person who has died and cannot be identified from the data.
explain: Personal data is data about a living person who can be identified from the data. These are human beings.

q: Does the Data Protection Act 2018 include GDPR?
options: No, the two are completely unrelated
Only for data held in manual records
No, GDPR replaced the DPA 2018 entirely
explain: The slide states that the Data Protection Act 2018 'includes GDPR', and that you should read the DPA 2018 alongside GDPR.
flag: Slide says DPA 2018 'includes' GDPR. In real law the DPA 2018 supplements and tailors the GDPR rather than containing it. Follow the slide.

q: Which body enforces the Data Protection Act in the UK?
explain: The Information Commissioner, the ICO, enforces the DPA in the UK.

q: Is the following statement correct? Personal Data shall not be transferred to a country outside the EEA unless that country ensures an adequate level of protection for the rights and freedoms of data subjects in relation to the processing of personal data.
explain: This is Principle 8, Transfer Abroad, quoted from the slide.

q: Is the following statement correct? Personal data shall be adequate, relevant and excessive in relation to the purposes for which they are processed.
explain: Principle #3 says adequate, relevant and NOT excessive.

q: Is the following statement correct? Personal data shall be obtained for one or more specified and lawful purposes, and may be further processed in any manner the controller chooses.
explain: Principle 2 says the data shall not be further processed in any manner incompatible with that purpose or those purposes.

q: Is the following statement correct? Putting personal data on the internet counts as a world-wide transfer.
explain: The Principle 8 slide says "putting on the internet = world-wide transfer".

q: Which principle number covers the transfer of personal data abroad?
explain: Principle 8 covers Transfer Abroad. Principle 7 is security, Principle 6 is the rights of a data subject and Principle 5 is retention.

q: Which principle covers the rights of a data subject?
explain: Principle 6 covers the rights of a data subject. Principles 1-5, 7 and 8 are obligations on Data Controllers.

q: Under the DPA principles, which set of principles places obligations on Data Controllers?
explain: Principles 1-5, 7 and 8 are the obligations on Data Controllers. The rights of Data Subjects are Principle 6.

q: Under Principle 6, a data subject can normally access data held on them within how many days, and with a fee of up to what?
explain: The slide says you can "access any data held on you, normally within 40 days, and fee up to £10".
flag: The slide figures differ from current law, where the GDPR gives one month and is normally free. Follow the slide.

q: According to the lecture, in which year was the Data Protection Act first passed?
explain: The slide says "Data Protection Act 1984. Updated in 1998, 2018."
flag: Slide 5 lists the DPA as 1994, 1998 and 2018, while slide 6 says 1984. Slide 6 is the explicit history, so slide 5 may be a typo.

q: In what year is the General Data Protection Regulation dated in the lecture?
explain: The IT law list and the DP overview give "GDPR 2016" and "General Data Protection Regulation 2016".

q: Which Act is dated 1990 in the lecture's list of IT law?
explain: The slide dates are CMA 1990, FOI 2000, RIPA 2018, and DPA 1994, 1998 and 2018.
flag: The slide dates RIPA as 2018, which differs from real law where it is 2000. Follow the slide.

q: Which year is given for the Freedom of Information Act in the lecture?
explain: The slide says "Freedom of Information, FOI 2000".

q: Who is a Data Controller?
options: The body that enforces the Act in the UK
Anyone contracted to do some data processing under another's instructions
The person(s) or organisation who holds the data or controls the processing
The individual who is the subject of personal data
explain: The Data Controller is the person or organisation who holds the data or controls the processing. The second option describes the Data Processor and the first describes the Data Subject.

q: Who is a Data Processor?
options: The individual who is the subject of personal data
The person who runs the public Register
Anyone in an organisation contracted to do some data processing under the data controller's instructions
The person or organisation who controls the processing
explain: The Data Processor is anyone in an organisation contracted to do some data processing under the data controller's instructions.

q: Which of the following is NOT an exemption listed in the lecture?
options: Direct marketing by the data controller
explain: The listed exemptions are National Security, Personal, Domestic and Recreational usage, Prevention and detection of crime, Journalistic, literature or artistic purposes, and where another statute authorises disclosure.

q: Which of the following is NOT something a Data Controller must notify the Information Commissioner about under the DPA 1998?
options: The salaries of the staff who process the data
What types of information are held for what purposes
Who the information is obtained from
Who the information is disclosed to
explain: Notification covers types of information held for what purposes, obtained from WHO, disclosed to WHO.

q: Sending unsolicited emails to individual consumers is an offence against which regulations?
explain: SPAM to individual consumers, and not to businesses, is an offence against PECR, which the ICO regulates.

q: In the lecture, what does 'compliance' mean?
options: Just enough to comply with the law
Going beyond the law to protect all data
explain: "Compliance" means just enough to comply with the law. "Best practice" means a good understanding within the law.

q: Which statement about the main improvements in GDPR is NOT correct?
options: Consent is now opt-in, and evidence must be kept.
Consent is now opt-out and may be implied.
The data controller must be able to demonstrate compliance.
The data controller is clearly responsible for compliance.
explain: GDPR brings accountability principles and a higher standard for consent, which is opt-in with evidence kept.

q: Is the following statement correct? GDPR has extraterritorial effect, so any UK company doing business with the EU will still need to comply.
explain: The post-Brexit slide says GDPR has extraterritorial effect, so non-EU countries are also affected.

q: Is the following statement correct? After Brexit, UK companies doing business with the EU no longer need to comply with GDPR.
explain: Any UK company doing business with the EU will still need to comply.

q: Where is the Information Commissioner's Office based, according to the lecture?
explain: The ICO address is Wycliffe House, Water Lane, Wilmslow, Cheshire, SK9 5AF.

q: What penalty does the lecture say you face if you are not exempt and don't follow the law?
options: Loss of the right to hold personal data for one year
explain: The summary says that if you are not exempt and don't follow the law, you will be penalised with fines or imprisonment.

q: Which statement about Principle #7 (Security) is NOT correct?
options: Appropriate technical and operational measures shall be taken.
It applies only to data held on paper.
Measures are taken against accidental loss, or destruction of, or damage to, personal data.
Measures are taken against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data.
explain: Principle #7 requires appropriate technical and operational measures against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.

q: Which statement about Principle #5 is correct?
options: Personal data shall be kept indefinitely if it is secure.
Personal data shall be kept for at least five years.
Personal data shall be accurate and where necessary kept up to date.
Personal data shall not be kept any longer than is necessary for the purpose(s) it is processed.
explain: Principle #5 is retention. 'Accurate and kept up to date' is Principle #4.

q: Which principle states that personal data shall be accurate and where necessary kept up to date?
explain: Principle #4.

q: How does the lecture describe the data covered by the DPA 1998?
options: Personal data held or processed in automated form AND some manual records
Only data held in automated form
explain: The DPA 1998 covers personal data held or processed in automated form AND some manual records.

q: Who maintains the register that data controllers appear on?
explain: The ICO page lists "The Data Protection Register" for data controllers. The DPA 1998 slide says controllers notify the Information Commissioner and are published on a public Register.

q: DPA Principle #1 states personal data shall be processed fairly and lawfully. Which of the following are included in Principle #1 as conditions for processing personal data?
options: to perform a contract with the individual
carry out a public function under statutory powers
to protect the vital interests of the data subject
to maximise the controller's commercial profit
pursue legitimate interests of the data controller unless prejudicial to the interests of the data subject
explain: Slide 12 lists consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public function under statutory powers, and legitimate interests of the controller unless prejudicial.

q: Which of the following are conditions for processing SENSITIVE data under Principle #1?
options: necessary under a legal obligation in the context of employment
pursue the legitimate commercial interests of the data controller
necessary for medical purposes, undertaken by a health professional
where the information has been deliberately made public by the data subject
explain: Sensitive data needs extra care and higher security. The conditions include explicit consent, employment legal obligation, made public by the data subject, medical purposes by a health professional, and racial or ethnic monitoring, among others.

q: Under Principle #6, which rights does the data subject have?
options: to be paid a fee by the controller for holding their data
to compensation for damage or damage and distress in (mis)use of personal data
to know the purpose(s) for which personal data is held
to request an assessment of whether the DPA is being complied with
to access any data held on them
explain: Slide 20 lists these rights. There is no right to payment for holding data.

q: Under Principle #6, which rights does the data subject have?
options: to have incorrect information erased if the data controller won't correct it
to appoint the data processor for the data controller
to prevent processing which causes substantial damage or substantial distress
an explanation behind the logic of automated decisions
to have any dispute over correctness recorded and visible with the record
to set the annual fee for the Register
explain: All of the first four appear on slide 20.

q: Which of the following are exemptions under the DPA?
explain: The exemptions are National Security, Personal, Domestic and Recreational usage, Prevention and detection of crime, Journalistic, literature or artistic purposes, and where another statute authorises disclosure.

q: Which of the following are exemptions under the DPA?
explain: All five are listed on the exemptions slide.

q: Principle #7 (Security) requires appropriate technical and operational measures against which of the following?
options: unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data
destruction of or damage to personal data
lawful disclosure to the data subject
explain: Principle 7 requires measures against unauthorised or unlawful processing, and against accidental loss of, destruction of, or damage to personal data.

q: Under the DPA 1998, which of the following was a Data Controller obligated to do?
options: be published on the public Register
explain: Slide 10 lists notify the Information Commissioner, public Register, follow 8 principles, annual fee.

q: What must a Data Controller notify the Information Commissioner about?
options: for what purposes it is held
what types of information are held
explain: Notification covers what TYPES of information are held, for what PURPOSES, who it is obtained from and who it is disclosed to.

q: Which of the following appear in the lecture's list of IT law?
explain: All six are on the I.T. Law slide.

q: Which are direct mail opt-out services named in the lecture?
explain: The direct mail opt-out services are the Mailing, Fax and Telephone Preference services.

q: By the end of the lesson, you should be able to do which of the following?
options: describe the obligations of Data Controllers
describe the EIGHT data protection principles
describe the Computer Misuse Act offences
outline the scope of the Data Protection Act 2018
explain: Learning objectives slide.

q: According to the lecture, what do the data protection laws outline?
options: the rights you have about your data
the 'privacy' you can expect around data storage
the price organisations may charge for storing data
the responsibilities others have to look after it carefully
explain: Slide 6 says data protection laws outline the rights you have about YOUR data, the responsibilities others have to look after it carefully, and the "privacy" you can expect around data storage.

q: Which of the following are main improvements in GDPR?
options: consent may be implied from silence
evidence of consent must be kept
the data controller must be able to demonstrate compliance
the data controller is clearly responsible for compliance
explain: The main improvements are accountability principles and a higher standard for consent, which is opt-in with evidence kept.

q: Which of the following are examples of 'processing' personal data?
explain: Processing is anything you do with personal data, such as hold, store, gather, delete and modify.

q: Which of the following are categories of sensitive personal data?
explain: Sensitive personal data covers racial or ethnical origins, religious believes, political opinions, physical or mental health, sexual preferences and criminal records.

q: Which statements about SPAM in the lecture are correct?
options: SPAM might also fall into the DPA 2018
PECR is regulated by the ICO
Sending unsolicited emails to individual consumers is an offence against PECR
The offence applies to emails sent to businesses
explain: SPAM to individual consumers, and not to businesses, is an offence against PECR, which the ICO regulates. It might also fall into the DPA 2018.

q: Which statements about GDPR after Brexit are correct?
options: UK organisations need to comply with GDPR
Non-EU countries are not affected by GDPR
GDPR applies to all EU countries and citizens
A UK company doing business with the EU still needs to comply
explain: Slide 24.

q: Why does the lecture say you should be interested in data protection?
options: You need to know where to go for further advice
You may need to assert your own rights
You may need to apply it to your final project, e.g. software or surveys
You may need to advise others as to what is legal or illegal
explain: Slide 4 lists all five.

q: In which years was the Data Protection Act enacted or updated according to the lecture's history of the Act?
explain: The Data Protection Act came in 1984 and was updated in 1998 and 2018.
flag: Slide 5 lists the DPA as 1994, 1998 and 2018, while slide 6 gives 1984, 1998 and 2018. Follow slide 6.

q: Principle #3 states personal data shall be adequate, relevant and not excessive. Which of the following are required by Principle #3?
options: not excessive in relation to the purposes for which they are processed
explain: Principle 3 says data must be adequate, relevant and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which they are processed.

q: Which of the following are the five Big Five (OCEAN) personality traits?
explain: OCEAN stands for Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism.

q: The seminar asks for the impacts on 5 categories of issues. Which of these are the categories?
explain: The seminar asks for impacts on 5 categories of issues, which are Ethical, Legal, Social, Professional and Systems.

q: What weighting does the in-class test carry in the module assessment?
explain: Element 010 Part 1, the in-class test, is worth 20%, and Part 2, the individual report, is worth 80%.

q: How long is the individual report and how much is it worth?
explain: Element 010 Part 2 is the individual report of 2000 words, worth 80%.

q: When is the individual report due and how is it submitted?
explain: Submission is via CANVAS at 2pm on Friday of week 12.

q: Which pair describes the Neuroticism trait?
explain: Neuroticism is described as sensitive and nervous versus secure and confident.

q: Which statement about the Big Five traits is NOT correct?
options: Agreeableness is described as friendly/compassionate vs. challenging/detached.
Extraversion is described as friendly/compassionate vs. challenging/detached.
Openness to experience is described as inventive/curious vs. consistent/cautious.
Conscientiousness is described as efficient/organized vs. easy-going/careless.
explain: Extraversion is outgoing and energetic versus solitary and reserved. Friendly and compassionate versus challenging and detached describes Agreeableness.

q: Which statements about the module assessment are correct?
options: Part 2 is a 2000-word individual report worth 80%
Part 1 is an in-class test worth 20%
The report is submitted via CANVAS
It is one single graded assessment element (Element 010)
The report is submitted by email
explain: Slide 14.

q: How many Facebook users' personally identifiable information was given to Cambridge Analytica, according to the article?
explain: Facebook gave access to PII of more than 87 million users to Cambridge Analytica.

q: In 2013, researchers at which institution analysed volunteers' Facebook personality tests?
explain: In 2013 researchers at the University of Cambridge's Psychometrics Centre analysed the results of volunteers who took a personality test on Facebook.

q: How many US participants did the 2013 Cambridge research draw in?
explain: The research drew in 350,000 US participants. The figure of 3.5 million is Kosinski's later sample base.

q: What does GSR stand for in the article?
explain: A second research project was reportedly started by Global Science Research, GSR, in cooperation with Cambridge Analytica.

q: Which platforms did GSR use for its personality quiz?
explain: The quiz ran on Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform and Qualtrics, a survey platform.

q: Until when did the Facebook Open API give access to users' friends' data, according to the article?
explain: Access to friends' data was available through the Facebook Open API until May 2015.

q: How many data points on how many US adults did Cambridge Analytica build?
options: 50,000 data points on 2.3 million US adults
5,000+ data points on 230 million US adults
500 data points on 87 million US adults
explain: '5,000+ data points on 230 million US adults'.

q: What was 'Project Alamo'?
options: A Facebook privacy law proposed by Senator Klobuchar
A targeted-messaging campaign paired with OCEAN analysis, used for the election campaign of President Trump
The GSR quiz run on Mechanical Turk
explain: The OCEAN analysis was paired with targeted messages in 'Project Alamo', employed for the election campaign of President Trump.

q: Facebook was being investigated by the FTC for violating what?
explain: Facebook is being investigated by the Federal Trade Commission, the FTC, for violating a 2011 consent decree.

q: Which senators put forward the CONSENT Act (S.2639)?
explain: The CONSENT Act, S.2639, comes from Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ed Markey of Massachusetts, both Democrats.

q: Which bill was introduced by Senator Amy Klobuchar?
options: Social Media Privacy Protection and Consumer Rights Act of 2018 (S.2728)
explain: S.2728 was introduced by Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat from Minnesota.

q: The California privacy bill adds limits on selling data on users younger than what age?
explain: The bill adds limits to selling data on users younger than 16 years of age.

q: Which of the following are the four headings of the core principles of privacy and data protection in the article?
explain: The headings are Public transparency, Disclosure for users, Control and Notification.

q: Which of the following does the CONSENT Act require or do?
options: bans all sale of user data
explicit opt-in consent before platforms use, share or sell PII
new reporting requirements in case of a data breach
requires the FTC to establish privacy protections for customers of online edge providers
explicit notification any time data is gathered, shared or sold to a third party
explain: The bill requires explicit opt-in consent and notification, adds breach reporting, and requires the FTC to establish privacy protections.

q: As few as how many voters in a few states are said to be enough to tip election results with individualised messages?
explain: Tipping the scale in a few states with as few as 100,000 voters is sufficient to impact election results.
